strings.name: Shehbaz Sharif
strings.summary: Shehbaz Sharif is a Pakistan Muslim League–Nawaz politician who led Punjab's government on three occasions, first became prime minister in 2022 and formed another government in 2024. His record spans infrastructure, international financing and coalition politics. Assessing his economic policies requires distinguishing financing approvals, actual disbursements and reform outcomes, while considering parliamentary support separately from disputes over national elections.
strings.coverageNote: Information checked through 18 November 2026. Parliamentary and government records underpin the office chronology, and IMF announcements supply financing terms. Official accounts from both sides of the 12 November 2026 Antalya meeting support his recent activity and current office. Party and opposition posts in older biographies are treated historically.
strings.influence.rationale: Moved from governing Punjab to Pakistan's premiership, participating in economic stabilization, infrastructure and regional diplomacy.
strings.facts.f1.label: Birth and education
strings.facts.f1.value: Born on 23 September 1951 and from Lahore, he graduated from Government College Lahore. The official passages reviewed do not specify his subject, degree level or graduation year, so these details are not added. His brother Nawaz Sharif also served as prime minister; their careers must be distinguished.
strings.facts.f2.label: From provincial assembly to federal government
strings.facts.f2.value: He entered the Punjab Assembly in 1988 and the National Assembly in 1990, then returned to the provincial assembly in 1993 as opposition leader. His Punjab chief-minister periods were 1997–1999, 2008–2013 and 2013–2018, with an interruption under Governor's Rule in 2009.
strings.highlights.h1.title: International financing: amounts and conditions
strings.highlights.h1.text: The IMF approved a roughly US$3 billion Stand-By Arrangement in 2023 and a separate roughly US$7 billion Extended Fund Facility arrangement in 2024. Their durations and review mechanisms differ; approval does not mean the entire amount arrived immediately. Financing entails fiscal, energy and other reforms and does not itself establish that debt problems are resolved.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Government formation and electoral disputes
strings.highlights.h2.text: In the 2024 parliamentary election for prime minister, he received 201 votes against his opponent's 92. Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf and others alleged fraud in the preceding general election; election authorities denied it. The parliamentary tally is verifiable, while the allegations should remain attributed, contested claims.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Meeting Erdoğan in Antalya
strings.timeline.t1.text: He met Türkiye's president during COP31. Both governments confirm the meeting took place; Pakistan's account lists trade, investment, defence and energy cooperation. Intentions to advance cooperation do not mean every project has been completed.
strings.timeline.t2.title: IMF approves a 37-month financing arrangement
strings.timeline.t2.text: The IMF Executive Board approved an approximately US$7 billion Extended Fund Facility arrangement, making about US$1 billion immediately available. The announcement was published on 27 September; Board approval, publication and subsequent instalments are distinct stages.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Taking the oath for a second premiership
strings.timeline.t3.text: On 3 March the National Assembly elected Sharif with 201 votes, against 92 for Omer Ayub; he took the oath the next day. Parliament elected the head of government, rather than voters directly electing a prime minister nationwide.
strings.timeline.t4.title: IMF approves a nine-month Stand-By Arrangement
strings.timeline.t4.text: The Executive Board approved approximately US$3 billion, with about US$1.2 billion immediately available and the remainder phased and subject to review. This financing arrangement belonged to his first premiership and is distinct from the 2024 Extended Fund Facility.
strings.timeline.t5.title: First elected prime minister by the National Assembly
strings.timeline.t5.text: Following the fall of Imran Khan's government, the National Assembly elected Sharif with 174 votes. His first premiership lasted until August 2023. The proceedings establish his election that day and do not substitute for an oath-ceremony record.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Becoming National Assembly opposition leader
strings.timeline.t6.text: He led the opposition in the federal parliament until becoming prime minister in April 2022. The consulate's biography retains older passages with an April 2022 cutoff; these describe historical service and do not establish that he still holds that post.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Returning to Punjab's government
strings.timeline.t7.text: He again became chief minister and was re-elected in 2013. Provincial assembly records show that Governor's Rule introduced on 25 February 2009 interrupted the provincial government's offices; the measure was revoked on 30 March. This career period therefore cannot be described as ten wholly uninterrupted years in office.
strings.timeline.t8.title: First becoming chief minister of Punjab
strings.timeline.t8.text: Following service in the provincial assembly and as opposition leader, he first headed Punjab's government. This term ended during the October 1999 military coup, more than two decades before he entered the federal premiership.
